vignette:
He is a 65-year-old African man who has spent most of his adult life working in retail, the kind of job that keeps him on his feet and in contact with strangers all day. Before the storm, he describes himself as steady and practical, someone who goes to work, comes home, checks on his wife, and keeps to routine. He and his wife have built a quiet life together, and he has long taken pride in being dependable.

Everything changes when the natural disaster hits his community with little warning. He remembers the sky turning an unnatural color, the wind rising so quickly it seems to have a mind of its own, and the first sounds of things breaking outside. He is at home when the danger begins, and what lingers most in his memory is not a single dramatic image but the feeling of helplessness as the power goes out, the house shakes, and he cannot tell whether the next sound will be the roof giving way or something crashing through the windows. He stays close to his wife, trying to sound calm for her, though inside he is certain that something terrible is about to happen. When the worst passes, he comes away alive, but his sense of safety does not return with the daylight.

In the weeks that follow, he moves through the aftermath as if he is still waiting for the next blow. He cannot stop scanning the sky and listening for changes in the wind. Loud rain, sirens, or even strong gusts make his body tense before he has time to think. He finds himself checking doors and windows repeatedly, often more than he needs to, and he sleeps in short stretches, waking at the smallest sound. At night he lies awake replaying the storm in fragments, especially the moments when he felt trapped and unable to protect his wife. He does not talk much about it at first. He tells himself that an older man should be able to handle hardship, but the memories return on their own, often when he is trying to rest or when the weather shifts. He begins to feel irritable and on edge, and his wife notices that he startles easily and snaps at minor frustrations.

He returns to work in retail, but the job no longer feels simple or familiar. The store’s emergency alerts, the sudden opening and closing of automatic doors, and the rumble of delivery trucks all pull his attention away from customers. He finds himself watching the ceiling, thinking about whether the building is secure, whether the weather outside is changing, whether he should be somewhere else. Concentration becomes harder, and he sometimes loses track of what a customer has asked him. He feels embarrassed by this and tries to cover it with silence and efficiency. He keeps working because routine helps him, yet he also begins to feel detached from the people around him. Coworkers chat, laugh, and complain about ordinary things, while he carries a private sense that the world is less predictable than it once seemed.

As time goes on, he notices that he avoids anything that reminds him too directly of the disaster. He turns off weather reports sooner than he used to. If a storm is mentioned on the news, he changes the channel. He hesitates when clouds gather, and he plans errands around the forecast. He no longer enjoys sitting outside during heavy wind or rain, which had once been part of the rhythm of his days. Even conversations with neighbors about storms or repairs leave him tense. He hates feeling this guarded, but he cannot seem to relax into the present. A part of him remains alert for danger, as if alertness alone might keep his family safe.

His wife remains one of the few people he lets see how deeply the experience has affected him. In private, he admits that he still feels ashamed of how frightened he was, and that shame makes it harder to speak. He worries about appearing weak, especially after a lifetime of being the one others rely on. At times he becomes sad in a quiet, withdrawn way, sitting for long periods without doing much. He says he feels older than his years, as if the storm took something from him that he cannot name. Even so, he continues to go to work, return home, and keep to the habits that still give his days shape, carrying the memory of the disaster with him in a way that is woven into nearly everything he does.
